tips_and_tricks: Know how to analyze data tables and charts — they are especially handy when looking at stimulus questions, which make up a large portion of the multiple choice and free response portions of the test.

The correct answer to multiple choice questions is often more general and ties directly to what the key unit, as a whole, is about. Go with your gut once you choose an answer; you're often right the first time!

On FRQs, always restate the specific number, trend, or variable from the stimulus in your answer — vague answers that don't reference the given data rarely earn the point even if the reasoning is correct.
Practice writing FRQ answers in complete, cause-and-effect sentences ("X causes Y because Z") — readers award points for the mechanism, not just the right vocabulary word.
For calculation questions, always show your work and include units — an unlabeled number is a common way to lose an otherwise-earned point.
When a question says 'identify AND explain,' you need both parts to earn credit; identifying the correct term alone is usually only half the point.
Environmental legislation FRQs (Unit 5-related) often ask you to name a specific act (e.g. Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, CERCLA) — memorize what each one actually regulates, not just its name.
For 'propose a solution' FRQ parts, always pair your solution with one realistic economic, social, or political tradeoff — many rubrics award a separate point specifically for the tradeoff.
Review energy-pyramid and 10% Rule math every unit — questions from Unit 1 resurface throughout the exam as a supporting concept in later units.
Don't skip Unit 5 and Unit 9 in your final review — land use and global change consistently produce some of the highest-point-value FRQs on the real exam.
